headline: Per-second billing on max(request, actual) for physical CPU cores and GiB of RAM, with no pause state. Modal's pricing page labels the CPU unit 'Physical core (2 vCPU equivalent)', and the sandbox guide says '1 core = 2 vCPUs'. Battleships prices the same dollar figure as one vCPU-hour, so its vCPU-hour rate is 2x Modal's documented vCPU-equivalent rate.

cpuUnitSettlement.question: Does Modal bill per physical core equal to 2 vCPU?
cpuUnitSettlement.answer: Yes on the billing unit: Modal prices sandbox CPU per physical core and states that one physical core is equivalent to 2 vCPUs, so the documented vCPU-equivalent rate is half the core rate ($0.070956/vCPU-hour vs $0.141912/core-hour). The pages do not establish how many CPUs the guest actually sees for a given cpu= value, and that was not tested; Battleships reports a benchmark where cpu=N yields N guest CPUs.

evidence.quote: Physical core (2 vCPU equivalent)
The cpu parameter specifies physical CPU cores (1 core = 2 vCPUs), and memory specifies MiB
Note that each physical core is equivalent to 2 vCPUs as offered by AWS or GCP.

ephemeralDisk.note: There is no separate disk meter. The sandbox filesystem is a fixed 512 GiB quota; asking for more disk raises the memory request at 20:1, so it is billed at the memory rate. Sandbox docs say the disk size cannot be increased.

evidence.quote: A per-container disk quota that defaults to 512 GiB.
Disk requests are billed by increasing the memory request at a 20:1 ratio. For example, requesting 500 GiB of disk will increase the memory request to 25 GiB, if it is not already set higher.
Sandboxes have the same disk limits as other Modal containers, and their disk size cannot be increased.

volumes.note: Volumes are the persistent filesystem that outlives a sandbox.

billedWhileStopped.value: no stopped state; compute accrues only while the sandbox runs
billedWhileStopped.note: Modal documents no paused or stopped state: a sandbox is running or finished, and CPU/memory are billed per second on max(request, actual). That a finished sandbox accrues no compute is inferred from per-second billing plus the finished state; no Modal page states 'terminated bills nothing' in those words. Volumes and snapshots bill separately.

hermesAgent.status: documented terminal backend in Hermes; no Modal-side template or guide found
hermesAgent.summary: Hermes Agent documents Modal as one of its six terminal backends. Hermes itself still runs on your own machine or server; Modal only runs the shell commands the agent issues, one sandbox per task, with an optional filesystem snapshot between sessions. That is not an always-on hosted agent: Modal sandboxes have a 24-hour maximum lifetime and no pause.
steps: Install Hermes locally (the official installer or pip).
Set terminal.backend to modal and size the container, e.g. `hermes config set terminal.backend modal`.
Provide Modal credentials: MODAL_TOKEN_ID + MODAL_TOKEN_SECRET, or a ~/.modal.toml file.
Run `hermes`. Each task's terminal commands execute in a Modal sandbox; with container_persistent the filesystem is snapshotted on cleanup and restored next session.
hermesAgent.nonCoderDashboard: No. The Modal dashboard shows sandbox metrics and invoices, but creating a sandbox is code (Sandbox.create) or CLI (`modal shell` attaches to one that already exists).

evidence.quote: Runs commands in a Modal cloud sandbox. Each task gets an isolated VM with configurable CPU, memory, and disk. Filesystem can be snapshot/restored across sessions.
Required: Either MODAL_TOKEN_ID + MODAL_TOKEN_SECRET environment variables, or a ~/.modal.toml config file.
This preserves filesystem state, not live processes, PID space, or background jobs.
You can change this by passing a timeout of up to 24 hours to the Sandbox.create(...) function.

openClaw.summary: OpenClaw's own hosting page lists a provider picker, Render and an experimental Cloudflare Containers template; Modal is not among its documented deployment targets, and Modal's documentation has no OpenClaw or Hermes page.

evidence.quote: Deploy OpenClaw on a cloud server or VPS.

deploy.alwaysOnVerdict: Not a fit for an always-on personal agent. Sandboxes are capped at 24 hours and there is no pause; an idle but running sandbox bills its full request. A 24/7 agent needs a separate always-on host, with Modal used only as the command sandbox.

notVerified: No account was created and no sandbox was started; signup, invoice and dashboard behaviour are from documentation only.
Snapshot storage is billed but no rate is published, so it cannot be costed.
The per-container maximum CPU and memory are enforced but not published.
Whether the guest actually sees two CPUs per `cpu` unit was not tested; Battleships reports a benchmark where it does not.
